messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Known People: Related people, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sameer sits rigidly in the chair, his medic’s uniform immaculate, a stark contrast to the chaos he describes. For months, the world has been closing in on him, a process so gradual he almost didn’t notice until the walls were touching his shoulders. It all began a year ago, but the memories feel as if they are happening now, not in the past. He remembers the specific heat of that evening, the way his ex-partner, David, had come home from the base gym. The sharp, animal smell of sweat had filled their small apartment, an odour that Sameer now finds unbearable. David had been wearing a grey, sleeveless t-shirt, the kind Sameer has since purged from his own wardrobe, unable to even look at the fabric. The argument that followed was a blur of motion and hot, searing pain, but certain fragments remain burned into his mind. He can still feel the phantom ache in his ribs where David’s knee had connected, a physical echo that returns with startling clarity whenever a memory breaks through. When he tries to speak about it, the words refuse to form; it’s a memory made of sensation and scent, not language.

In the aftermath of leaving David, Sameer believed he had escaped. He met and married a kind woman, transferred to a new post, and tried to rebuild. But the past followed him. The scent of body odour on a crowded bus can send a jolt of terror through him so potent he has to get off at the next stop, gasping for air. He stopped exercising entirely, unable to tolerate the feeling or smell of his own sweat, which felt like a betrayal by his own body. His once athletic frame has softened, another mark of the man he no longer is. The avoidance has bled into his work. As a military medic, he is surrounded by authority, but the sight of a commanding officer or a military police officer now triggers a silent, sickening panic. He sees David’s unassailable confidence in their posture, hears the same tone of command in their voice. He feels small, powerless, just as he did on the floor of his apartment.

His life has become a carefully curated set of safe zones. Home is manageable, but only certain rooms. Work is a minefield he navigates with clenched fists. He has withdrawn from friends, from his new wife’s family, and even from his own relatives who remind him of David’s, the people who knew and did nothing. He is certain they see the same weakness in him that he sees in himself. There is something fundamentally wrong with him, he has come to believe, a deep, structural defect for allowing it to happen. He is a soldier, a medic trained to handle the worst of human injury, yet he could not protect himself. This thought is a constant, corrosive presence. It has leached the meaning from everything he once valued. Saving lives feels pointless when his own feels so irrevocably broken. The injustice of it all is a bitter pill; David faced no consequences, his career flourishing while Sameer’s world crumbles.

At night, the threat feels most immediate. Sleep offers no refuge. He lies awake for hours, his body rigid, listening. Every creak of the floorboards, every car door slamming in the street, sends a shockwave through his system. He has to stay alert, certain that danger is just outside the door. Sometimes, a memory will ambush him in this state of exhausted vigilance. He won’t just remember; he will be back there, the rough texture of the carpet against his cheek, the smell of sweat overwhelming him, feeling as if it’s all happening again for the very first time. It was after one such night, when the sound of his wife dropping a spoon in the kitchen made him cry out and dive for cover, that he finally made this appointment. He came seeking help not with any real hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified that this is all his life will ever be: a man in a uniform, trapped in a room, waiting for a blow that has already landed.
